name: Philipp Schmid (Google DeepMind) context engineering piece
publisher: Philipp Schmid, Staff Engineer / AI developer-relations lead at Google DeepMind, publishing on his personal blog (philschmid.de), not an official Google DeepMind channel
date_published: 2025-06-30 (original piece, 'The New Skill in AI is Not Prompting, It's Context Engineering'); a follow-up, 'Context Engineering for AI Agents: Part 2', was published 2025-12-04
source_type: independent practitioner essay (personal blog by a Google DeepMind staff engineer; not a corporate/official Google publication, but he writes from that vantage point)
claim_value: Defines context engineering as 'the discipline of designing and building dynamic systems that provides the right information and tools, in the right format, at the right time, to give a LLM everything it needs to accomplish a task.' States that prompt engineering is about crafting a single perfect instruction string, while context engineering is 'a far broader' systems discipline that subsumes it, alongside RAG (external/up-to-date knowledge), short- and long-term memory, and tool/function definitions. Central qualitative claim: 'Most agent failures are not model failures anymore, they are context failures.' No quantitative benchmark figures are given.
claim_definition: A practitioner's taxonomy/opinion piece, not a measured result. It asserts a definition and a causal attribution (agent failures = context failures, not model failures) based on Schmid's own observation of agent-building practice, not a controlled study.
evidence_category: practitioner anecdote / survey opinion (first-person synthesis of practitioner experience and other practitioners' public commentary, not an empirical study)
reproducibility: Not applicable - no benchmark or code-dependent empirical claim is made. The piece is conceptual/advisory.
publisher_sells_relevant_product: yes (indirectly) - Schmid works at Google DeepMind, which sells Gemini and Gemini-based agent tooling; the piece's framing (LLMs need the right context/tools/format, agent failures are context failures) directly supports the case for Google's agent-building tools and Gemini's tool-use/context-handling features, even though the post is published on his personal site rather than an official Google channel and does not explicitly name-drop Gemini products as the solution. [uncertain on degree of commercial intent vs personal thought leadership]
conflict_notes: No numeric figure exists in this source to create a factual discrepancy with secondary citations. One nuance worth flagging for the article: this piece (June 30, 2025) predates Anthropic's widely-cited 'Effective context engineering for AI agents' post (September 2025) by about three months, and it already cites LangChain's earlier blog post on context engineering plus tweets from Andrej Karpathy and Tobi Lutke as its own inspirations - meaning the term's circulation through LangChain/Karpathy predates both the Schmid and Anthropic posts, so neither major lab coined it independently.
relationship: Complicates the 'prompt engineering is dead, context engineering is what matters now' framing in a specific way: Schmid explicitly frames context engineering as broader than and inclusive of prompt engineering (prompt engineering is a subset/component, the single-string-instruction part), not a successor that makes prompting obsolete. This is a more moderate position than framings that declare prompt engineering dead.
derivative_of: Explicitly cites and builds on a prior LangChain blog post on context engineering, and credits tweets by Andrej Karpathy and Tobi Lutke (Shopify) as direct inspiration for using the term. The December 2025 follow-up ('Part 2') explicitly credits Peak Ji (Manus AI) and Lance Martin (LangChain) plus 'latest industry research' on context rot and multi-agent coordination as what it extends.
register: practitioner/engineer, with secondary relevance to enterprise AI teams building agents; written in an accessible, implementation-focused style rather than academic register.
confidence: secondary_unverified - findings are drawn from direct WebFetch of the original post plus corroborating web search results (for dates, affiliation, and the Part 2 follow-up); the primary post's text was fetched and quoted directly, giving reasonably high confidence on the definition and core claims, but the characterization of commercial intent and the exact relationship to Anthropic's post are inferred rather than stated by Schmid himself.
notes: Confirmed via independent search that Schmid is a Staff Engineer on Google DeepMind's AI developer-experience/developer-relations team (joined 2025), which supports the 'major AI lab voice' framing in the task description even though the post itself runs on his personal domain, not a deepmind.google or research.google URL. The December 2025 'Part 2' piece was found but not deeply fetched in this pass; it postdates Anthropic's post, so only the June 2025 original is relevant to the 'predates Anthropic' angle.
already_cited: no - this specific Schmid piece is not referenced in article_ideas.md's 09-27 'Context engineering didn't retire the prompt' entry or the AGENTS.md thought/counterpoint as far as the available context shows. [uncertain, since those files were not directly re-read in this pass]
new_angle: Establishes that the 'context engineering' framing was already circulating among practitioners (LangChain, Karpathy, Tobi Lutke) and picked up by a second major lab voice (Google DeepMind's Schmid) a full three months before Anthropic's September 2025 post, which is the piece's main use for the 'did labs converge independently or echo each other' question: the timeline points to convergence-via-circulation (LangChain and Twitter/X practitioner chatter first, then Schmid, then Anthropic) rather than two labs independently arriving at the same term. It also offers a slightly softer stance than 'prompt engineering is dead': prompting is a subset of context engineering here, not its replacement.
